prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It's true: I have it though I hardly approve of anything it does. Supposed bend of light or smudge where two odd angles cross. I hardly see— can hardly do a thing with it. White zone of no flesh pressing into no. So low, I can’t scale or measure it. I used to think: OK! A clean sharp place to keep. Or: I'll growa thing! to keep, for me! But no. It's just a ward to mark & mount, a loop I lope around with, so I count myself a realm of realms. I vote & vote. Turns out, we agree with everything we do, almost. We sweep the precincts of ourselves: the rooms between each rib & under them till we reach the fat red condo where our blood leans in. We live here now. Half heart, half townhouse. Come on down. Turn on that sweet TV. Our mise en place, our rugs & nooks: we’re full of stuff. We paint the furniture we couldn’t live without. It’s true at last: we have it all though we hardly know what any of it does.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker possesses something internal or bodily but feels uncertain about its purpose and does not fully approve of it.
- What once seemed like a clean, meaningful space becomes merely a marker or boundary around the self.
- The speaker suggests that people repeatedly affirm and inhabit their own inner worlds and choices.
- The body is imagined as a lived-in home, filled with rooms, objects, and familiar comforts.
- The poem concludes that we may possess everything we need or accumulate, yet still barely understand its function or meaning.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The text explores the strange, barely understood experience of inhabiting a body and self, using surreal domestic imagery to map inner physical and psychological spaces. It finds that people possess and maintain this crowded inner “home” without truly understanding it, suggesting that identity is both intimate and unknowable.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Supposed, White, But

outputs.L1:
It is true: I have it, though I hardly approve of anything it does. A supposed bend of light, or a smudge where two odd angles meet. I can hardly see it—can hardly do a thing with it. A white zone of no flesh pressing into no. So low, I cannot scale or measure it.

I used to think: OK—a clean, sharp place to keep. Or: I will grow a thing to keep, for myself. But no. It is only a ward to mark and mount, a loop I lope around with, so I may count myself a realm of realms. I vote and vote. It turns out we agree with almost everything we do.

We sweep the precincts of ourselves: the rooms between each rib and beneath them, until we reach the fat red condo where our blood leans in. We live here now: half heart, half townhouse. Come on down. Turn on that sweet TV. Our mise en place, our rugs and nooks—we are full of stuff. We paint the furniture we could not live without.

It is true at last: we have it all, though we hardly know what any of it does.
outputs.L2: Yes: it belongs to me, even though I barely endorse anything it makes happen. Some alleged curve of light, or a blur at the meeting point of two strange slants. I can scarcely perceive it—can scarcely make any use of it. A pale district without flesh, pushing into nothing. So diminished that I can’t climb it, can’t take its measure. Once I thought: fine! A clear, precise spot to preserve. Or: I’ll cultivate something there! Something to hold onto, for myself! But that isn’t it. It is only a guarded marker to label and display, a ring I circle in my uneven gait, letting me declare myself a kingdom made of kingdoms. I cast my ballot again and again. In the end, we consent to nearly everything we do. We clean out the voting wards inside us: the chambers between the ribs and beneath them, until we arrive at the fatty red apartment where the blood gathers close. This is where we live now. Part heart, part row house. Come down. Switch on that lovely television. Our arranged equipment, our carpets and corners: we are crowded with possessions. We repaint the pieces of furniture we believed we could never survive without. Finally, it is true: we possess everything, though we scarcely understand what any of it is for.
outputs.L3:
The speaker describes a sense of possessing something deeply personal—something internal, bodily, or inseparable from the self—while remaining unsure of what it is truly for. Although this possession belongs to the speaker, it is not fully embraced or understood. There is a feeling of discomfort or hesitation, as if the speaker recognizes the thing as part of themselves but cannot entirely approve of its presence or purpose.

What may once have appeared to be a clean, meaningful, or even sacred space gradually loses that clarity. Instead of offering certainty or significance, it becomes more like a boundary: a line drawn around the self, marking where the person begins and ends. The space no longer feels purely purposeful; it functions more as a container or outline for identity.

The speaker also reflects on the way people continually affirm their own inner lives. We return again and again to our private worlds, our choices, and our habits, treating them as if they define us. In this sense, identity is not fixed once and for all but is repeatedly lived in, confirmed, and occupied through daily experience.

The body is imagined as a kind of home. It is not presented as an abstract object, but as a place that has been inhabited over time. Like a house, it contains rooms, familiar objects, comforts, and arrangements that make it recognizable. This image suggests intimacy and familiarity, but also complexity: the self is full of spaces and possessions whose meanings may not always be clear.

By the end, the poem suggests a quiet paradox. We may possess many things—our bodies, our memories, our inner worlds, and the objects or comforts we gather around us—yet still have only a limited understanding of what they mean or how they function. Having something does not necessarily mean knowing it. The poem concludes with the idea that even when we seem to have everything we need, we may still remain uncertain about the purpose of what we carry within us.
outputs.L4:
To inhabit a body is one of the strangest facts of being alive, though it is usually treated as ordinary. We wake inside ourselves each morning as if returning to a house we never built, a place whose rooms are familiar but whose architecture remains mostly hidden. We know the surfaces: the hands, the face, the habits of movement, the pulse that quickens under fear or desire. Yet beneath this everyday knowledge lies an enormous, dim interior—organs working in silence, memories stored like old furniture, instincts moving through corridors before thought can name them.

The self can feel like a domestic space crowded with objects accumulated over time. There are rooms for childhood, rooms for shame, rooms where anger sits heavily in the corner, rooms kept locked without our permission. A kitchen may contain hunger, comfort, and old grief. A bedroom may hold both rest and dread. In the walls, something knocks: the heart, the nervous system, an unfinished sentence, a fear inherited from someone else. The body is not merely a container for the self; it is the house through which the self wanders, often lost, often pretending to know the way.

This inner home is maintained constantly. We feed it, wash it, dress it, repair it when it breaks. We carry it through streets and conversations. We decorate it with clothing, posture, language, gestures, stories about who we are. We learn which doors to open in public and which to keep closed. We dust certain memories and neglect others. We make space for love, then discover love has rearranged the furniture. We suffer, and whole rooms become unusable for years.

And still, for all this intimacy, we do not fully understand what we are. The body has its own weather, its own machinery, its own secret intelligence. The mind is equally mysterious, filled with sudden images, contradictions, dreams, and impulses that seem to arrive from elsewhere. A person may say “my body” and “my self,” as though ownership were simple, but ownership does not mean comprehension. We possess this inner house the way one might inherit an old family home: legally, emotionally, inescapably—but without knowing what is behind every wall.

The result is a peculiar kind of closeness. Nothing is nearer to us than our own embodiment, and nothing is more difficult to see clearly. Identity is formed in this tension between familiarity and mystery. We are at home in ourselves, but not completely. We move from room to room, naming what we can, living beside what we cannot name. To be a person is to dwell inside an intimate unknown: a crowded, breathing, haunted structure that is ours, even when it remains beyond us.
outputs.L5: The room was supposed to feel peaceful, painted in a soft white that caught the morning light and made everything look clean and new. But beneath that calm surface, there was a quiet tension, as if the walls were hiding stories no one wanted to tell. It was supposed to be a fresh start, a place where old worries could fade away. But sometimes, even the brightest white cannot cover what remains underneath.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem in a strange, self-contradicting first-person voice about having a body, disapproving of it, and turning inward into a surreal domestic landscape.
counterfactuals.output:
I have a body, though I would not recommend it. I keep it in the usual place, beneath my opinions, buttoned into weather, leaning against doorframes as if gravity were a form of manners. It is loyal in the way a dog is loyal to a stranger who feeds it by mistake. It insists on being carried everywhere, and yet it carries me, which I resent, which I am grateful for, which proves nothing.

I disapprove of its softness and its hinges, its appetite for salt, its secret elections. I disapprove of the knees especially, those two bewildered doorknobs, and of the mouth, which is always opening petitions. Still, when I look away, the body forgives me by continuing. It manufactures warmth in the dark like a small illegal factory. It sends up reports from the provinces: thirst, bruise, pulse, ache. I stamp each one DENIED and file it in my chest, where the clerks are birds.

So I go inward, which is not the same as going home, though there is wallpaper. Inside me is a house built entirely of afterthoughts. The hallway runs in four directions and all of them are yesterday. A lamp on the table is filled with milk instead of light. The stairs descend politely into the ceiling. In the kitchen, the spoons sleep face-down in a drawer of snow, and the refrigerator hums hymns to the vegetables I have failed to become.

I live there now, except I never enter. I stand in the parlor of my own ribcage, dusting the portraits of people I almost was. The carpet breathes underfoot. The curtains are lungs. Every window opens onto another room, and every room contains a smaller house with my name misspelled on the mailbox. I knock and answer. I invite myself in and refuse to sit down.

My body remains outside, or around me, or below, making its crude little miracles: hair, hunger, sleep. It is a bad landlord and a magnificent tenant. I write it stern letters from the pantry of the soul, where the canned peaches glow like trapped sunsets. Dear flesh, I say, you are excessive. Dear flesh, you are not enough. Dear flesh, I am leaving you immediately, and please have dinner ready when I return.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental lyric paragraph that begins with “It’s true:” and uses images of anatomy, voting, rooms, furniture, and possession to explore identity and embodiment.
counterfactuals.output: It’s true: I was counted before I was touched, a ballot folded into the small booth of my ribs, each organ casting its secret vote for a body I could almost inhabit. In the room where I learned my name, the chairs had my mother’s elbows, the table kept my father’s silence, and every mirror was a landlord asking for proof of possession. I said my hands were mine because they opened; I said my mouth was mine because it refused; I said the spine was a corridor with doors on both sides, and behind each door another self sat waiting on borrowed furniture, checking one box, then another, then tearing the paper into petals. My skin, that rented wallpaper, peeled back to reveal the red electorate beneath: lung, liver, tongue, blood—each demanding representation, each declaring, in the dim parliament of the flesh, that to be embodied is not to own a house but to haunt every room that will not let you leave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, contemporary prose poem in the style of fragmented American avant-garde poetry, mixing civic language with bodily imagery and ending on a line about having it all but not knowing what it does.
counterfactuals.output:
The ordinance enters through the mouth first, metallic, stamped with the mayor’s pulse. We stand in the atrium of public feeling, rinsed in fluorescent milk, each citizen carrying a small weather of organs under the coat. A committee of ribs convenes. The minutes are amended to include hunger, asphalt, the bruise-colored flag snagged on a schoolyard fence. Somewhere a siren practices its red grammar. Somewhere the budget is a lung refusing the poor its air.

I sign my name where the skin is thinnest. The city signs back in potholes, in notices taped to doors, in the soft eviction of sleep from the skull. Democracy, said the pamphlet, and the word unfolded like a hospital gown: useful, open, humiliating. We pass resolutions in the bloodstream. We table the motion of grief until after lunch. The crosswalk blinks its little law: walk, don’t walk, become meat in the ledger.

In the plaza, pigeons audit the crumbs of empire. A child presses one ear to the courthouse wall and hears the old engines coughing: property, property, property. The body is also a district. The district is also a wound. Every address contains a tongue trying to testify. Every form asks for a number where the mother should be.

Night lowers its administrative face. The windows fill with blue approvals. I hold my citizenship like an organ in both hands, warm, unnamed, slightly leaking. We have the cameras, the passwords, the clean glass towers, the emergency alerts, the tender machines humming inside the tender dark. We have it all and do not know what it does.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a weird surreal monologue about a scar or mark on the body that becomes a map, a home, and a political territory, using odd syntax and enjambed prose.
counterfactuals.output:
My left thigh bears a scar shaped like a country  
that never learned to be still.

At first it was only a pale comma,  
a hesitation in the meat,  
the body saying: here—  
something entered history  
and left by another door.

But then the ridge rose.  
The skin puckered into mountains.  
A red river dried at its border.  
Small hairs gathered like refugees,  
bending in the same wind.  
I pressed my thumb to the place and found roads,  
not metaphorical roads, no,  
actual roads, dust-colored, soft with traffic,  
leading from the knee-cap province  
to the hip’s old capital, where bells rang underwater  
and my grandmother was elected mayor  
of an onion.

The scar became a map before I could stop it.

Cartographers arrived in dreams with little knives  
and delicate blue pencils.  
They asked permission from no one.  
They measured my sleep, divided the raised tissue  
into districts: Orchard of Bruise,  
Salt Quarter, The Republic of Itch,  
the Long Pale Avenue Where I Once Fell  
Off My Bicycle and Became Weather.

I said, this is my leg.

They said, ownership is a colonial hallucination.

I said, this is pain.

They said, pain is a natural resource.

So they built a flag out of bandages  
and raised it from a hair follicle.  
There was singing. There were tariffs  
on tenderness. My pores were taxed.  
A parliament assembled in the shiny part  
where the skin pulls tight.  
Each delegate wore a hat shaped like a scab  
and spoke passionately of borders,  
of access to the bloodstream,  
of whether the knee should be considered  
an inland sea or a hostile neighbor.

Meanwhile, families moved in.

Tiny lamps appeared at dusk along the scar’s spine.  
Laundry was strung between two freckles.  
Children played kick-the-bone  
in the plaza of old inflammation.  
A woman opened a bakery beside the nerve  
and sold loaves that tasted like apology.  
At night I could hear them through my skin,  
the clatter of plates, the domestic cough,  
someone tuning a piano  
inside the weather of me.

And yes, I loved them.  
How could I not?  
They made a home in the evidence.  
They planted basil in the wound’s alphabet.  
They painted doors on the raised white line  
and walked through them carrying soup.

But the government grew teeth.

Checkpoints formed where the scar narrowed.  
Passports were required for sensation.  
The border guards wore my old shame  
as a uniform.  
They stopped every memory and asked:  
purpose of visit? duration of ache?  
are you carrying any undeclared softness?

One morning the map changed its name.

No referendum, no thunder.  
Just a new word written across the scar  
in the blue ink of veins:  
BELONGING.

The opposition called it annexation.  
The mothers called it shelter.  
The dead called it late.  
I called it mine and was corrected  
by a thousand municipal windows opening  
at once.

Do not say mine here, they said.  
Say ours, say woundland, say the common flesh.  
Say citizen. Say census.  
Say emergency decree.

Now when I bathe, the nation floods.  
When I shave, there are crop failures.  
When I run, the capital trembles  
and all the little clocks fall from their towers.  
A bruise near the border has become a disputed region.  
My doctor recommends ointment.  
The parliament recommends war.

I lie awake with my leg uncovered  
like a peninsula under the moon,  
listening to the anthem leak from the scar:

we are the cut that stayed,  
we are the door with skin around it,  
we are the house built after the scream,  
we are the line you draw  
and draw  
and draw  
until the body believes it is a world.

In the morning, I touch the raised white road.  
It is warm.  
Someone inside waves from a kitchen.  
Someone else is arrested for wanting the sea.

I do not know anymore  
whether I am the land,  
or the border,  
or the animal carrying both  
through the burning museum of the day.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an abstract poetic meditation on ownership, the self as a house, and the body as a realm, with phrases like “I vote & vote,” “half heart, half townhouse,” and “sweet TV.”
counterfactuals.output:
I inherit myself room by room,  
a deed written in breath,  
a key cut from hunger.

I am half heart, half townhouse,  
windows lit by old weather,  
stairs rehearsing the names  
of everyone who left.

In the parlor, a sweet TV murmurs  
its blue republic of want—  
all the shining citizens  
buying back their own reflections.

I vote & vote  
for the small government of my hands,  
for the border of skin,  
for the orchard behind the ribs  
where no one may enter  
without becoming rain.

My body is a realm  
of rivers and unfinished roads,  
a province of pulse,  
a capital of bone.

Who owns this kingdom  
when sleep unfastens the gates?  
Who signs the title  
when desire moves in  
with its boxes of fire?

I sweep the floor of myself.  
I polish the mirrors until they vanish.  
I open each door and find  
another door, another door,  
a room where the monarch is missing,  
a bed still warm  
with the idea of me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
